scenario: A consultant uploads the same client brand guide and contract into a new chat every week before asking for help with that client.
question: Which feature would best remove this repeated work?
options: Research, so Claude finds the brand guide and contract again each week
A Project for the client, with the guide and contract saved as knowledge
An incognito chat each week, so the client's files aren't kept on record
One running chat for the client, left open so the files stay in context
explanation: B is correct: the same files recur in every chat, and a Project's knowledge is used across all its chats, so he uploads them once. A is wrong because Research runs slower multi-source searches for questions; it doesn't hold a stable reference set. C is wrong because incognito keeps nothing for reuse, so he would still upload weekly. D is wrong because one endless chat drifts and uses more of the limit.

scenario: A strategy lead on a Pro plan needs an overview of how five competitors have changed their pricing in the past year, drawn from many sources, and wants to check the evidence behind it.
question: Which Claude feature best fits this task?
options: A plain chat answering from what Claude already knows, with no searching
An artifact, since the overview will be long and shared with the board
Account instructions telling Claude to be thorough and cite its sources
Research, with web search on, then open the sources it found
explanation: D is correct: the answer is spread across many sources, which suits Research's searches that build on each other; it needs a paid plan and web search, and she opens the sources her conclusions rest on. A is wrong because Claude's existing knowledge misses last year's price changes. B is wrong because an artifact is an output format, not a way to gather sources. C is wrong because instructions don't give Claude new sources.

scenario: An office manager has four Claude tasks this week and wants to use the lightest feature that fits each one.
question: Which task is the best fit for a plain chat, rather than an artifact or a Project?
options: Building a reusable onboarding checklist the team will update monthly
Rewording one email to sound more polite
Running a three-month client engagement with shared reference documents
Creating an interactive budget calculator to share with colleagues
explanation: B is correct: rewording one email is a short, one-off task, and a plain chat is the lightest fit. A is wrong because a checklist the team updates monthly is something to keep and edit, which suits an artifact. C is wrong because months of work with shared reference documents suits a Project. D is wrong because an interactive calculator shared with colleagues is an artifact.

scenario: A cinema chain's insight team must sort 5,000 short survey comments into eight fixed categories by tomorrow morning. The categories are clear and each comment fits one of them.
question: Which model family fits this job best?
options: Opus, so the trickier edge-case comments are handled safely
Sonnet for the whole job, since it is the everyday choice for most work
Haiku, the fast, lower-cost family built for high-volume sorting
Whichever model in the menu shows the newest version number
explanation: C is correct: sorting thousands of items into fixed groups is simple, repeatable and high-volume, which is Haiku's job, and the overnight deadline rewards speed. A is wrong because Opus is slower and uses more of the limit, and clear categories leave few edge cases. B is wrong because Sonnet is slower than this simple sorting needs. D is wrong because version numbers change and don't tell you a family's job.

scenario: A strategy director needs to work through a complex pricing decision with many interacting assumptions and trade-offs, once per quarter.
question: Which model family is the best fit?
options: Opus, the most capable of the three families, suited to complex multi-step reasoning
Haiku, so the director can quickly try many more pricing options
Sonnet at its default setting, since it's the everyday choice
Any of the three families, since they reason about pricing equally well
explanation: A is correct: interacting assumptions and trade-offs call for long, multi-step reasoning, and a quarterly, high-value decision justifies Opus's extra time and usage. B is wrong because speed matters little for a once-a-quarter decision, and Haiku is weaker on complex reasoning. C is wrong because Sonnet suits everyday writing and analysis, not the hardest problems. D is wrong because the families differ in how deeply they reason.

scenario: A port authority's operations team writes a two-page weekly report from structured shift notes. It needs decent quality and has to go out the same afternoon.
question: Which model family is the best everyday fit for this report?
options: Opus, because a report read by senior managers deserves the deepest model
Haiku, because it is the fastest family and time is short
Haiku at a higher effort level, to get speed and depth together
Sonnet, which balances speed and capability for everyday writing
explanation: D is correct: a short report from tidy notes is everyday writing with a same-day deadline, Sonnet's balance. A is wrong because Opus is slower and uses more of the limit for reasoning this report doesn't need. B is wrong because Haiku suits high-volume, simple tasks such as sorting, not a quality report. C is wrong because higher effort slows Haiku and uses more of the limit, giving up the speed it was chosen for.

scenario: A marketing team will generate descriptions for 2,000 products. They're unsure which model to use.
question: What is the best approach?
options: Use the most capable model for the whole batch, just to be safe
Pick any model, since short descriptions come out much the same
Test a sample on a lighter model and step up where quality falls short
Use the balanced family for the whole batch, since it's the safe middle
explanation: C is correct: volume multiplies every choice, so a sample on the lightest model that might work shows whether it is enough before 2,000 runs. A is wrong because the heaviest model may spend far more time and usage than the task needs. B is wrong because picking at random isn't a decision; the families differ in speed and cost. D is wrong because the middle family is still a guess, untested on real items.

scenario: An events coordinator at a conference organiser sets effort to Max for every task, including quick replies to speaker emails.
question: What is the main drawback of this habit?
options: Quick replies get slower and use up the limit sooner, with no better result
Higher effort makes Claude's answers shorter and less detailed
Max effort switches off web search for the rest of the chat
There is no drawback, since Max is the most thorough level
explanation: A is correct: effort sets how thorough each response is, and higher levels take longer and use more tokens, so routine replies gain nothing while the limit arrives sooner. B is wrong because higher effort makes Claude more thorough, not briefer. C is wrong because effort doesn't change which tools are available. D is wrong because thoroughness costs time and usage that quick replies don't repay.

scenario: An analyst runs a weekly report on a fast model. Recently the reports have needed complex judgements about conflicting data, and reviewers are finding shallow conclusions. The team's other tasks haven't changed.
question: What is the most appropriate change?
options: Keep the setup and add "think harder about the conflicts" to the prompt
Move the team's whole workload onto the most capable family to be safe
Turn on thinking for the fast model and leave its effort level alone
Raise effort, or step up the family, for this report and check the conclusions
explanation: D is correct: the deciding constraint is that only this report changed, so extra depth belongs there, and checking shows whether more effort is enough. B is the close alternative, but the other tasks are unchanged, so moving them wastes time and usage. A is wrong because prompt wording isn't the lever; effort is. C is wrong because thinking can't be turned off on current models, so effort is the setting to change.

scenario: After a three-hour planning chat, Claude starts mixing up decisions made early in the conversation.
question: What is the best next step?
options: Keep going in the same chat and correct each mix-up as it appears
Ask for a summary of decisions and open items, then start a new chat with it
Delete the chat and start a fresh one without carrying anything over
Switch to the fastest model so the long chat starts responding more quickly
explanation: B is correct: long chats drift as early details compete with later ones, and they use more of the limit; a summary keeps the decisions and a fresh chat clears the rest. A is wrong because the chat keeps growing and the mix-ups come back. C is wrong because it throws away the decisions already made. D is wrong because a different model doesn't shorten an overloaded chat.

scenario: A team discussed the agreed launch date in one chat in their Project. In a new chat in the same Project, Claude doesn't know it.
question: Why does this happen, and what is the lasting fix?
options: A Project keeps context in its first chat, so continue the work there
Rename the Project after the launch so Claude links its chats together
Ask Claude in each new chat to search the earlier chat for the date
Chats don't share conversations, so add the date to Project knowledge
explanation: D is correct: chats in a Project share its knowledge and instructions, not each other's conversations, so saving the date there reaches every future chat. A is wrong because the first chat has no special role, and continuing it only makes it longer. B is wrong because Claude can't see the Project's name or description. C is wrong because chat search is paid-only and has to be repeated in every new chat.

scenario: A team manager at an insurance broker works in her team's Project. She wants to ask one sensitive question about a staff matter without it being used in or added to memory, but she wants to keep the chat in her history.
question: What should she do?
options: Turn off Memory in the + menu for that chat, before the first message
Start an incognito chat inside the Project for just this question
Ask the question normally, then tell Claude to forget it afterwards
Add an account instruction telling Claude not to remember sensitive topics
explanation: A is correct: turning memory off for one chat works inside Projects, keeps the chat in her history and stops it using or adding to memory, but it has to be set before the first message. B is wrong because incognito chats aren't available in Projects and aren't saved to history. C is wrong because asking afterwards doesn't undo what was already shared. D is wrong because the per-chat switch, not an instruction, controls memory.

scenario: A zoo's education team has two years of monthly school-visit bookings in a CSV file. The head of learning wants a chart for trustees showing the exact monthly totals.
question: How should she get the chart from Claude?
options: Paste the numbers into a chat and ask Claude to estimate the trend
Use Research so Claude cross-checks the bookings against other sources
Upload the CSV and have Claude run code on it, with code execution on
Ask for a chart artifact describing the bookings, without the data file
explanation: C is correct: exact totals mean calculating from the real data, and code execution lets Claude analyse an uploaded CSV with Python and chart it, provided the Code execution and file creation setting is on. A is wrong because an estimated trend isn't an exact total. B is wrong because Research gathers web and connected sources, not her own figures. D is wrong because without the file Claude has no real numbers to chart.

scenario: A translation agency wants each client delivery report to follow its house layout. Reports are written in many different client Projects, and the layout shouldn't affect other chats.
question: Where should the agency put the layout?
options: In account instructions, so it applies in each conversation
In a custom skill that Claude loads when a report is requested
Pasted into each chat by whoever asks for a delivery report
In the instructions of the busiest client Project the agency has
explanation: B is correct: a skill is a saved procedure that loads only when a task calls for it and works across Projects; it needs code execution switched on. A is wrong because account instructions apply to all conversations, so the layout would leak into other chats. C is wrong because pasting by hand drifts from colleague to colleague. D is wrong because Project instructions reach only that one Project's chats.

scenario: A bid manager at an IT consultancy has Research on her paid plan and Google Docs connected. On the train with only her phone, she needs an answer that draws on the web and the team's past bids in Google Docs; it's due tomorrow.
question: What should she do to get an answer that uses both sources?
options: Start Research on her phone now, since it searches the web and connectors
Start Research from the web or Desktop app once she is at her laptop
Start Research on her phone and ask it to include the team's Google Docs
Use web search on her phone now, since Research is too slow for this
explanation: B is correct: the deciding constraint is the phone. Research on Mobile searches only the web and silently skips connectors, while on web and Desktop it also searches tools such as Google Docs; with a deadline of tomorrow, waiting costs little. A is the close alternative but would miss the past bids. C is wrong because asking doesn't add connectors on Mobile. D is wrong because web search can't reach her Google Docs either.

scenario: An operations lead at a cycle-hire scheme has four tasks this week and wants to use Opus where its extra time and usage pay off.
question: Which task most needs Opus?
options: Reconciling three years of conflicting ridership data using judgement
Tagging 400 returned-bike photos as damaged or undamaged for repairs
Reformatting a list of 120 docking stations into a sorted, tidy table
Drafting a short service-update email to members about roadworks
explanation: A is correct: conflicting sources over several years need multi-step reasoning and judgement, which is where Opus earns its extra time and usage. B is wrong because tagging hundreds of photos is simple, high-volume work that suits Haiku. C is wrong because reformatting a list is a simple, repeatable task for a lighter family. D is wrong because a short email is everyday writing that Sonnet handles well.

scenario: A recycling company's governance officer must turn well-structured notes into a 30-page monthly board pack within the hour. The content needs moderate reasoning, not deep analysis.
question: Which model family should she pick?
options: Opus, because a board pack is high-stakes and deserves the deepest model
Haiku, because the one-hour deadline makes speed the main concern
Sonnet, balancing speed and capability for substantial drafting
Opus at a lower effort level, to get depth while saving some time
explanation: C is correct: the deciding constraints are moderate reasoning and a one-hour deadline, which fit Sonnet's balance. A is the close alternative: Opus would also work, but it is slower and uses more of the limit for no gain here. B is wrong because 30 pages of board drafting goes beyond the simple, repeatable work Haiku suits. D is wrong because it is still the slower family, chosen for depth the task doesn't need.

scenario: A florist group's office manager uses Claude all day for quick, routine jobs such as rewording delivery notes and confirming staff rota swaps.
question: Which setting best suits these quick tasks?
options: Keep the model's default effort, or drop to Low or Medium
Set effort to Max so each reply is as polished as possible
Switch to the most capable family for each of these tasks
Turn thinking off so the replies come back more quickly
explanation: A is correct: for everyday tasks the default effort works well, and Low or Medium suit routine work and stretch usage. B is wrong because Max takes longer and uses more tokens with nothing to gain on short rewording. C is wrong because the heaviest family is slower and uses more of the limit. D is wrong because thinking can't be turned off on current models; effort is the setting to change.

scenario: A pricing analyst at a wine importer gives Claude a clear brief and the data. The answers are correct but shallow on the hardest step: weighing three exchange-rate scenarios.
question: What should she change first?
options: Switch to the fastest family so she can rerun the analysis more often
Lengthen the prompt and add "be thorough" before each step
Raise the effort level for this analysis and compare the result
Start a new chat and paste the same brief and data in again
explanation: C is correct: the brief is already clear and the answers are right but shallow, which is the gap effort closes; step up the family only if that falls short. A is wrong because the fastest family reasons less deeply. B is wrong because the brief isn't the problem, and wording doesn't change thoroughness the way effort does. D is wrong because a fresh chat with the same settings gives the same depth.

scenario: A logistics broker extracts 800 fields from delivery notes each day on Sonnet at High effort, and quality is fine. The manager wants it faster and cheaper, but the figures feed invoicing, so quality has to hold on every run.
question: What should the team do next?
options: Switch the whole job to Haiku from tomorrow, since extraction is its job
Test a sample of real notes on Haiku at default effort before switching
Keep Sonnet but drop to Low effort across the job straight away
Leave it on Sonnet at High, since the current setup already works
explanation: B is correct: the deciding constraint is that quality has to hold on every run, so a sample shows whether Haiku keeps it before invoicing depends on it. A is the close alternative: extraction suits Haiku, but switching untested risks errors reaching invoices. C is wrong because it also changes the job without checking quality. D is wrong because it ignores the manager's valid goal when a lighter option may well work.

scenario: A receptionist joins a dental practice group on the Team plan. She says Claude doesn't carry her preferences between chats, although it did on her personal Pro plan.
question: What is the most likely reason?
options: Memory is a consumer-plan feature, so Team accounts don't offer it
It's a known fault with new Team seats that support has to fix
Team chats are kept separate, so she should paste preferences each time
On Team, each member's memory stays off until she turns it on
explanation: D is correct: on Team and Enterprise, owners control whether memory is available (it is on for the organisation by default), but it stays off for each member until they turn it on; on Pro it is on by default. A is wrong because Team plans can offer memory. B is wrong because this is expected behaviour, not a fault. C is wrong because pasting works around a setting she can turn on.

scenario: A buyer at a bookshop chain deleted an old chat that contained a supplier's outdated terms. Claude still mentions those terms in her new chats.
question: What should she do to stop it?
options: Delete any other older chats that might mention the same supplier's terms
Tell Claude in a new chat to forget the supplier's old terms
Find and edit or delete that entry in Settings > Your Claude > Manage
Reset memory so everything is wiped and Claude starts again
explanation: C is correct: the deciding fact is that deleting a chat doesn't remove memory entries made from it, so the entry itself has to be edited or deleted. A is the close alternative, but deleting more chats leaves the memory untouched too. B is wrong because asking in a chat isn't how memory entries are removed; the Manage page is. D is wrong because Reset deletes all memory, including project memory, to fix one entry.
